q: You arrive late on the first evening and miss the skipper's safety briefing. What do you do before the boat leaves?
a: Ask the skipper to walk you through it
o: Read the boat's manual once you are under way
Ask another guest to sum it up on your watch
Nothing — you will pick it up as you go
why: You must know where the safety gear is before you sail, and only the skipper's briefing covers this boat.

q: You are packing for a week's charter from Lefkada. Which shoes do you take for deck work?
a: Deck shoes with non-slip, non-marking soles
o: Black-soled trainers with a deep tread
Flip-flops that dry quickly
Leather shoes with smooth soles
why: Soft non-slip soles grip a wet deck and leave no black marks; flip-flops come off your feet.

q: You must carry two fenders forward along the side deck while the boat rolls in a ferry's wake. How do you do it?
a: One at a time, holding on with your free hand
o: Both at once, hugged to your chest
Both at once, walking quickly forward
One at a time, steadying yourself on the boom
why: One hand for yourself, one for the boat — and the boom is no handhold, it swings.

q: What do you do to stay fit for your watches today?
a: Drink water often, before you feel thirsty
o: Drink only once you feel really thirsty
Swap water for cold beer — it is still fluid
Save the water until the end of the day
why: In heat you lose water all the time; thirst comes late, and alcohol dries you out further.

fig.title: Passage day, August
lines: Air 35 °C, little shade in the cockpit

q: This is what you find on your lifejacket. What do you do?
a: Hand it to the skipper and take another one
o: Wear it — red shows it is ready to fire
Wear it and rely on the oral tube instead
Blow it up by mouth to test, then wear it
why: A red indicator means the inflator may not fire; the jacket must be re-armed before use.

q: A wave fills the cockpit and your automatic lifejacket inflates. Later you let the air out. Can you wear it on your next watch?
a: No — it needs a re-arming kit fitted first
o: Yes — just let the air out and fold it
Yes, once it has dried in the sun
Yes — a spare charge fires next time
why: A fired jacket has an empty cylinder; it will not inflate again until it is re-armed.

q: Your friend finds her lifejacket's crotch strap uncomfortable and leaves it undone. What happens if she goes over the side?
a: The jacket rides up over her face as it inflates
o: The jacket will not inflate on contact with water
The cylinder fires early as she moves about
Nothing — the waist belt alone holds it in place
why: Without the crotch strap an inflated jacket slides up and can cover the face or come off.

q: Your skipper says lifejackets go on whenever there is a real risk of ending up in the water. In which of these do you wear yours?
a: The tender ride back to the boat after dinner ashore
o: Sitting in the cockpit while moored stern-to in harbour
Sleeping in your bunk during your off watch
Hosing down the deck while tied up in the marina
why: Night tender trips, often after a drink, are a classic way to drown — wear a lifejacket.

q: The skipper sends you forward to free a jammed furling line. Which side deck do you use?
a: Port — the high, windward side
o: Starboard — the low, leeward side
Starboard, holding the boom as you go
Either — the heel makes no difference
why: On the windward side a slip throws you onto the deck, not over the low guardrail.

q: You need to cross the cockpit to reach the cool box. What is the main danger to you?
a: An accidental gybe swinging the boom across
o: The genoa backing and stopping the boat
The mainsheet jamming in its block
The boat suddenly luffing head to wind
why: Running in a rolling sea, the boom can gybe without warning at head height — keep low.

fig.title: Downwind run
lines: Wind F4 from astern, following sea
Boat rolling, main out to starboard

q: You check this list after the skipper's briefing. What is still missing from it?
a: Where the first-aid kit and the bilge pump are
o: Where the spare bedding and towels are kept
How the plotter's tide page works
Which marina the boat will use tonight
why: A safety briefing covers the first-aid kit and the bilge pump too — ask if they were missed.

fig.title: Briefing — what you were shown
lines: Flares and liferaft: cockpit and stern

q: You are on deck all day in July with a cool breeze blowing. How do you protect yourself from the sun?
a: Hat, long sleeves, sunglasses, sunscreen topped up
o: Sunscreen once in the morning is enough
No cover needed — the breeze stops sunburn
Cover up only at the first sign of redness
why: Wind cools the skin but does not stop UV; the sun and its glare off the water burn all day.

q: You are helming at night as the wind rises, and the skipper tells you to clip on. Where do you clip your tether?
a: A strong point in the cockpit meant for it
o: The guardwire beside the wheel
The mainsheet traveller car
A stanchion next to the helm
why: Use a proper strong point: guardwires and stanchions can fail and the traveller car moves.

q: Your tether has two hooks. Clipped to the jackstay, you reach the mast and must move to the strong point there. How?
a: Clip the second hook on, then unclip the first
o: Unclip from the jackstay, then clip to the mast
Hold a shroud while you move the one hook
Unclip and hold the mast — it is only a minute
why: With two hooks you are never unclipped: always clip on before you unclip.

q: Rain starts and you put on your foul-weather jacket. Where does your lifejacket go?
a: Over the jacket, so it can inflate freely
o: Under the jacket, to keep it dry
Under the jacket, so it cannot snag on lines
Either way — it inflates the same
why: Under a jacket it cannot inflate properly and squeezes your chest; wear it on top.

q: The skipper's standing order is 'clip on at night'. You come up for your 22:00 watch on a calm, starry night. What do you do?
a: Clip on before you step out of the companionway
o: Skip it — the rule is meant for rough weather
Clip on only if you go forward of the mast
Skip it — the moon gives enough light
why: A night rule has no exceptions: someone who falls over in the dark is very hard to find.

q: What do you do before you leave the cockpit?
a: Lifejacket fastened, clip on, tell the helmsman
o: Lifejacket on, clip on once you reach the mast
Harness on; no lifejacket needed when clipped
Lifejacket on; clip on only if it gets worse
why: Clip on in the cockpit before you move, and let the helm know you are going forward.

fig.title: Reefing at night
lines: Skipper needs you at the mast
Spray over the deck, boat heeling

q: You want to go forward and secure the halyard. What do you do first?
a: Wake another crew member before you go
o: Go forward clipped on, without waking anyone
Go quickly unclipped, wearing your lifejacket
Go once the deck lights are switched on
why: Never leave the cockpit alone at night: if you fell in, nobody would know you were gone.

fig.title: Alone on watch
lines: A halyard has come loose at the mast

q: At night, in a moderate sea, your friend is seasick and needs to be sick over the side. What do you do?
a: Take her to the leeward rail, clipped on, and stay
o: Take her to the windward rail, the high side
Let her use the leeward rail, unclipped
Let her go to the leeward rail alone, for privacy
why: Be sick to leeward so it blows away — but clipped on and watched: that is the rail people fall over.

q: What do you advise your cousin?
a: Wear a lifejacket on deck whenever under way
o: None needed in calm water in daylight
None needed if she stays in the cockpit
Put one on only once the wind gets up
why: A non-swimmer wears a lifejacket on deck at all times under way, whatever the weather.
